report:
## Conclusion: No — Arthroscopy Does Not Help with Knee Osteoarthritis

The evidence consistently shows that arthroscopic surgery (including lavage and debridement) is **no more effective than placebo or conservative treatment** for osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee. Major guidelines now recommend against it.

### Key Evidence

1. **Sham-controlled trial (Moseley et al., NEJM 2002):** In a landmark randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 180 patients with knee OA were assigned to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or sham surgery (skin incisions only, no arthroscope insertion). At 24 months, there were **no differences** in pain or function between any groups. ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259))

2. **Kirkley RCT (2008):** Another randomized controlled trial found arthroscopy was **no more effective than placebo surgery** in improving pain or function in patients with moderate-to-severe knee OA. ([https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3))

3. **2024 systematic review:** Studies comparing arthroscopic knee surgery to conservative treatment for knee OA produced **inconsistent results at best**, with no clear superiority for surgery. ([https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12891-024-07813-3))

4. **Clinical practice guidelines:** An international guideline panel explicitly **recommends against** arthroscopic knee surgery in patients with degenerative knee disease, noting that financial incentives may explain why the procedure remains common despite evidence against its use. ([https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline))

### Summary

Despite being one of the most common orthopedic procedures, arthroscopy for knee OA has been shown in high-quality sham-controlled trials to provide **no meaningful benefit** over placebo. The consensus among evidence-based guidelines is that conservative treatments (exercise, weight management, medications) should be preferred, and arthroscopy should be avoided for uncomplicated knee OA.
